publicationTitle: Transactions of the South African Institute of Electrical Engineers
abstract: The great and growing importance of well-designed and adequate switchgear for the protection and control of electrical machinery, makes it unnecessary to apologise for presenting a paper on so well worn a theme. The main object in so doing is to pave the way to a thorough discussion — by users — of the advantages and failings of the various types of switchgear supplied — by manufacturers — to meet their requirements. It is hoped that a description of some forms of modern switchgear, with a few notes oh its development from the original elementary apparatus, and on the principles kept in mind in designing gear suitable for modern requirements, may induce those who have suffered to point out the defects to which their troubles were due, and thus assist the manufacturers, by showing what should be supplied and what avoided, in order to prevent similar trouble in the future.

abstract: Professor W. Buchanan (Member) : The present paper reminds one of the many discussions that took place some 15 to 20 years ago regarding the relative merits of alternating and direct current supply for town lighting, but it must now be admitted that considerable success has been attained with both systems. Since both the Ward-Leonard and the Three-Phase systems of winding seem to contain the elements necessary for success, the present controversy regarding their relative merits will no doubt reach a perfectly satisfactory conclusion. Although we may agree that it is preferable to use electricity instead of steam for all winding plants, it is very improbable that any one electric system will give the most economical results under all working conditions, — each case must be considered as a special problem, maximum economy being obtainable only by a careful study of the particular features and details of each system.

abstract: In view of the present day importance of Radio telegraphy — or, as it is more commonly called, “Wireless” — it is a little surprising that the nature and functions of the apparatus employed in actual practice are not more generally understood. To-night, instead of confining my remarks to the principles involved and adopting the usual method of demonstrating them by means of the familiar experimental instruments, I propose to describe to you in a general manner the apparatus comprising a Marconi plant of standard design. This I intend doing with the assistance of a series of lantern slides prepared from photos I have taken of the Marconi station now in operation on the Bluff at Durban. This station includes the latest Marconi apparatus, and presents wireless in a complete and up-to-date form. For the benefit, however, of those here this evening whose acquaintance with wireless may not have hitherto extended much beyond reading accounts of its achievements in the newspapers, I will first briefly, and as simply as I can, outline the fundamental principles involved, and describe in operation the transmitting apparatus of a similar, but less elaborate, plant, devoid of some of the complications of modern improvement. In order to keep the following remarks within the scope of this paper, it will be obviously impossible for me to attempt more than the simplest outline. Therefore, if my explanations are somewhat superficial, I can only hope you will recognise the difficulties I have to contend with in attempting to cover so much ground in such limited time.

publicationTitle: Transactions of the South African Institute of Electrical Engineers
abstract: Report of the Special Committee on the Use of Electricity in Mines. — In their report to the Home Secretary, the Special Departmental Committee appointed to inquire into the working of the existing specia rules for the use of electricity in mines, point out that the conditions have altered considerably since the rules came into force some five years ago and that they need revision. Whereas the early installations were all direct-current plant the tendency now is to adopt the three-phase system and this the Committee consider to be a change in the right direction. After receiving evidence from a large number of representative witnesses, the Committee have drawn up a proposed new code of rules which, they suggest should apply to metalliferous mines as well as coal mines. The rules relate to apparatus below ground only, with the exception of the switchgear at the pit-head controlling the underground distribution system.

publicationTitle: Transactions of the South African Institute of Electrical Engineers
abstract: Electric Power in Colleries. — A paper by Mr. F. Anslow, entitled, “Some Considerations affecting the installation of Power at Collieries,” was among those discussed at the meeting at Dunfermline of the Mining Institute of Scotland, on June 17th. Mr. Anslow, in dealing with existing steam plants at collieries, said that these were often destitute of condensing plant, partly on account of difficulties in running winding engines condensing, but he showed that in most cases, except where increased power is required, the cost of adding condensers to improve the economy was not justified. Where extensions are required, however condensing plant and exhaust, or mixed turbines driving electrical generators, will render considerable extra power available without extra steam being required from the boilers. Details were given of a case where an extra 500 KW. was thus made available. Even where a large proportion of steam plant is already condensing, considerable extra power can be obtained by the installation of mixed pressure turbo plant, and particulars were given of an example to illustrate this.

articleTitle: A suggested commutatorless direct current generator
publicationTitle: Transactions of the South African Institute of Electrical Engineers
abstract: (Member): I will first suppose that this machine is able to produce an E.M.F. and consider what some of the results will be following from the design. First, we have a 12 pole field producing bunches of lines running more or less radially through what might be termed the field distribution ring; and passing very rapidly through these bunches we have numerous very large and quite solid armature teeth — surely these teeth will heat up very considerably. Then conversely when the machine is running and the rotor is excited the armature teeth will carry round bunches of lines which will produce eddy currents in the field distribution ring. Again the excited rotor poles will, in proportion as the reluctance of the complete magnetic path rises and falls, generate an increasing and decreasing current in the field coils of the stator, and since all these coils are in series and wound with fine wire, the potential at the terminals will probably be excessive. Now most of these effects could be obviated by using a one coil field construction which would give a smooth field distribution, and such a design, based on the inventor's line of thought, can be made very much more simply and cheaply. I made a small rough model to see if any effect whatever could be obtained, but though I forced about 3 amp. through the fine wire windings there was no tendency to turn in either direction, nor could one feel any sense of lag when turning the model and then switching on the current.

abstract: (Member): I consider Mr. Herd's paper excellent; especially for the office shelf for reference. It is full of useful information, but I would like to remind him when he enlarges so ably upon the necessity of suitably choosing motors, that we are now in Johannesburg and not at Schenectady, and that not being able to wait six months for delivery, we have to be thankful for what we can get. With regard to running motors on unbalanced circuits, the same excessive heating effects have been noticed with three-phase transformers, and if the loss of balance cannot be helped then three single-phase transformers are more suitable. I think that perhaps too much stress is laid on the subject of out of balance circuits, because the tests were made with an artificially created out of balance ratio; under ordinary circumstances every three-phase motor added to a circuit tends to pull the phases into balance. The effects produced at the test, however, are sufficiently extraordinary to call for close attention, and very possibly many of the cases of excessive heating of motors running on small plants on these fields may be traced to this cause.

publicationTitle: Transactions of the South African Institute of Electrical Engineers
abstract: (C.) 435/10. Arthur Martin Ludwig Dammrich (1), Charles Hansen (2) Improvements m means for conveying and distributing water or other liquids in mines and the like. 3.9.10. This invention relates to means for conveynig and distributing water or other liquids in mines or any other place where the conditions met with are more or less similar to those in underground workings. The special object that the inventors have ha in view is to lay out or provide a water service in a mine, or any other place where the conditions are analogous, in such a way that the pipe system shall not be subjected to excessive hydraulic pressure whatever may be the vertical distance between the points of supply and the lowest point of the distributing system. It is claimed that the improved system is applicable for conveying and distributing water or other liquids to any depth without exceeding a safe pressure, such pressure, if so desired, not to exceed, say. 50 lb to the square inch or thereabouts. Briefly stated, the invention consists of supply tanks in each level fitted with a float, an electric contact for signalling when the tank is empty a tap for drawing off the water as required, and an overflow pipe near the top of the tank to act as an air vent and overflow outlet The main supply pipe is taken from the surface to the bottom of the first tank, and from a point in this tank, below the level of the overflow pipe, a pipe is taken to the bottom of the second tank which acts as the supply pipe to that tank. Similarly, the water is taken from level to level throughout the mine. It will be obvious therefore, that as long as the capacity of the overflow pipes fitted to the tanks is greater than that of the mail supply pipe, the hydraulic pressure in any section will not be greater than that due to the vertical head between the tanks in the levels above and below the section in question.

articleTitle: Atmospheric phenomena & their relation to the production of over-voltages in overhead electric transmission lines
publicationTitle: Transactions of the South African Institute of Electrical Engineers
abstract: (Associate) : Mr. G. V. Adendorff in his paper says — "It is well known that there is no electric force within a closed conductor, and the obvious method then is to completely surround the line in a metallic shield." This statement, though quite correct when statical charges only are under consideration, is by no means so when dynamical charges are dealt with as in the case of lightning discharges. In order to be sure of this point I have performed experiments (under Professor Buchanan's guidance) in the laboratory of the School of Mines, using a Whimshurst machine and Leyden jars to produce a miniature lightning flash, of the type known as the "B" flash, to use Sir Oliver Lodge's nomenclature. The first experiment was to see if one wire from a tin plate was sufficient to protect a second earthed wire under the tin plate : AB being the tin plate : earthed by means of AC : DE being the wire it was required to protect. When DE was close to AB it was found that a spark could be obtained between E and AB. A second wire was added from B to earth, to make the earthing of AB more symmetrical, but still a spark could be obtained between E and AB. To make the experiment yet more conclusive, the wire ED was surrounded by a metallic conductor — a piece of steel pipe. The connections of the apparatus were as shown in the diagram, Pig. 2. The pipe was connected to the tin plate to which the knob D was fixed by means of three copper wires, the object being to leave a space through which the gap EF could be watched. An electrostatic voltmeter was connected across the small gap EF. On a spark occurring across AB, a "B" flash occurs between C and D, and a small spark can be obtained between E and F. Thus the wire is not protected, although surrounded by a closed metallic conductor. A momentary deflection is produced on the electrostatic voltmeter.

publicationTitle: Transactions of the South African Institute of Electrical Engineers
abstract: The Action of the X-Ray in Large and Small Doses. — Since the discovery of the X-rays and their application to therapeutics, many and various results have been obtained from their use, results often quite contradictory in character, the explanations of which have at times been distinctly puzzling. It has been difficult in many instances to explain why in one case the use of the rays would cause degeneration and at others regeneration of similar tissues; why, for example, in one patient superflous hair would be removed and in another the use of the rays on a smooth skin would result in a profuse hirsute adornment. In recent years, however means have been devised of regulating the dose of the X-rays and of estimating in units the amount of radiation being administered in each case. This has made the study of the action more accurate and has enabled the illumination of several obscure points. In the Berliner klinische Wochenschrift for May 23, 1910, H. E. Schmidt reports a small series of experiments into the effect of various doses of the X-ray upon cell growth. Having soaked a number of beans in water for six hours he treated the different beans with different doses of rays, and then planted them. His results were quite uniform and demonstrated two points of interest. Whereas those beans which were treated with large doses of the rays were partially or completely inhibited in their growth, as compared to untreated control beans, those which received very small doses were distinctly stimulated; not only were the plants larger and more vigorous, but the flowers were larger and the resulting crop of beans better. From these findings Schmidt suggests that the same principle may apply to animal cells, and experiments which he carried out on an ulcer on the arm suggested that this is the case. If this be so, it is evident that in treating conditions in which healing is desired, as a sluggish ulcer, very small doses of the X-ray should be used, whereas in cases of malignant growth, where tissue destruction is required, large doses are needed, and small doses instead of destraying the neoplasm may do harm rather than good by stimulating it to renewed activity. — Electrical Review and Western Electrician, July 30. 1910, p. 234.

publicationTitle: Transactions of the South African Institute of Electrical Engineers
abstract: The author assumes that members are already acquainted with the essential features of the Ward-Leonard and Three-Phase systems, and this paper is, therefore, confined mainly to a comparison of costs. The great advantages of the Ward-Leonard system, particularly safety and ease of control, are well-known and generally admitted, but the opponents of the system frequently consider its apparently high first cost prohibitive. The author proposes to show that even granting that the first cost is higher than for the Three-Phase system, in very many cases this is largely counterbalanced by the difference in working costs It would, of course, be impossible m a short paper such as this to institute comparisons between all possible cases, and the author is well aware that in many instances the working costs of the Three-Phase may be as low as those of the Ward-Leonard system but he is of opinion that in the majority of cases, and more particularly where hoists are installed for winding from deep shafts and at high speed, the determining factor must be by all means that of safety and not of cost, although the author holds that the latter are more favourable with the Ward-Leonard, as will be proved to you later on. It will no doubt be possible to so improve the Three-Phase control as to make the system as safe as the Ward-Leonard, but a comparison of executed examples of each undoubtedly points to the superiority of the latter m this respect.

abstract: Electric Power in Collieries. — A paper with the above title was read before the Ruby Engineering Society by Mr. J. Miller on January 19th In the author's opinion, it is generally more profitable to instal generating plant at the colliery, but if the load consists mainly of haulage, with little pumping and ventilation, the load factor may be very low indeed, and the plant be running at low efficiency, so that it may be cheaper to take power from a supply company. The author gives figures for a 250-kw. colliery set. which gave a total output of some 25,000 units per month. The capital charges amounted to 0.725d. per unit, and the running costs to 0.438d. per unit, giving a to ta of 0.725d. per unit. These figures refer to a period when the set was only about a quarter loaded. Power was originally taken from a local supply company at the price of one penny per unit.

abstract: Control of Electric Winders. — In a paper read before the Manchester Section of the Institution of Electrical Engineers on December (5th Dr. E. Rosenberg (British Westinghouse Electric ∧ Manufacturing Co.) dealt with the control of electrically driven main winders. The author pointed out that, besides starting and stopping ordinary loads, it is often necessary to lower unbalanced loads, in which case the motor, if it be used at all, must work as a generator. If no tail rope is used, and the load on the up-going cage is just balanced by the load on the down-going cage, then the rope weight will, in the first half-trip, exercise a positive, and in the second half a negative torque, and the winding machine has at first to act as a motor and then as a brake.

abstract: (Associate Member): The author of this paper is evidently very much in favour of squirrel cage motors with auto starters. I cannot claim to have had extended experience with this type of motor, but the experience I have had, goes to prove that where motors are running fairly constantly (without much stopping and starting) then squirrel cage motors are the most efficient and economical. Where, however, frequent stopping and starting is required, then troubles commence, not usually in the motor itself, but in the starting device. The contacts are generally the source of the trouble. I think if manufacturers were to make auto starters with quicker breaks on the change over switches, less trouble would be experienced than is the case. Squirrel cage motors are certainly the best to use in the smaller sizes, for, with the smaller sized motors with the polar wound rotors and starter, either liquid or metallic, the brushes have either to remain on the slip rings all the time, or else the brush lifting and shortcircuiting gear, which has to be made in size somewhat proportional to the size of the motor, becomes more or less unreliable. My own experience is that several makers of really reliable motors fail to reach the same standard of reliability with their brush lifting gear as with the rest of their machine. Some of the best types of brush lifting gear have the brush holders faxed on square insulated rods which are decided in their action when rotated, and not given to slipping when the brushes are under tension. In some types, the brush lifting spindles are round and have an insulating bushing slipped over them. The brush holders are then placed on the bushing and clamped on, and are expected to fasten the bushing to the spindle: they may fasten in the factory, but after having been used a few times, the bushing starts slipping and the brushes give trouble through not having sufficient tension. In some cases of this description which have given trouble, the bushings have been fixed to the spindle with wooden pins and have since given no trouble.

abstract: Earth Return. — For more than a year a Commission of the Swiss Electrotechnical Society has had under observation the use of the earth as a return conductor between St. Maurice and Lusanne, and l'Industrie Electrique, quoting from a report of the Commission; states that the system has worked satisfactorily from the moment when it was put in regular service, without a single derangement. Direct current at 20,000 volts is used on the Thury system, with a single line conductor, the second line conductor having been idle during the past 14 months. No complaints have been made by the engineers of the Federal Railways, the compensating batteries installed at certain stations having absolutely prevented interference with the railway signals. — The Electrical Review, November 4, 1910, p. 764.

abstract: Licensing of Wiremen. — Some discussion took place at the annual meeting of the Victorian Institute of Electrical Engineers in Melbourne regarding the licensing of wiremen. Mr. Noel Murray, a member of the Council of the Institute, desired that the municipal authorities be approached in the matter, as at present there was an enormous amount of bad work being put in. The only way to obviate this, in Mr. Murray's opinion, was to issue licenses to the wiremen in the same way as is done with engine drivers and plumbers. which would give the authorities control over the men. If a man wired a building in a faulty manner, then he should have his license suspended for six or twelve months, and this would be the means of raising the standard of work in the wiring world. A man should also be made responsible for the material used as well as for the work done. Mr. P. Rosling, the newly-elected president of the Institute, stated that the committee had considered the matter, but nothing could be done without passing au Act of Parliament. He therefore suggested that the matter should be left over until the wiremen's wages board was settled. Mr. E. H. W. Westwood said that in Wellington (N.Z.) no wireman was allowed to touch the Council's mains unless he held a license, but he believed the whole thing had proved a failure. It was eventually decided to bring the matter before the council, who would report upon it at the next meeting. — The Australian Mining Standard, March 29, 1911, p. 310.
